speaker: Doctor
text:
Based on your liver function tests showing significantly elevated Alkaline Phosphatase and Bilirubin, along with the ultrasound finding of an enlarged, thin-walled gallbladder without stones, this strongly suggests a blockage in the bile ducts. Have you experienced any recent fever or chills, and is there any pain specifically in the right upper quadrant of your abdomen?

REQUEST TEST: Abdomen_CT_With_Contrast
REQUEST IMAGES: Ultrasound_Gallbladder_Duplicate

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: CT_Abdomen_With_Contrast: No acute findings; Ultrasound_Gallbladder_Duplicate: Enlarged, thin-walled gallbladder. No evident stones.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The CT scan and repeat ultrasound show no stones or acute findings, yet your labs indicate significant cholestasis (high bilirubin and ALP) with an enlarged gallbladder. This clinical picture suggests obstruction, likely due to a stone stuck in the cystic duct causing Mirizzi syndrome or a tumor. Do you have a history of pancreatitis, and have you noticed any lumps or masses in your neck or armpits?

REQUEST TEST: MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography)
REQUEST TEST: Tumor_Markers (CEA, CA 19-9)

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: MRCP: No obstruction identified; Tumor_Markers: CEA-Normal, CA_19-9-Normal

speaker: Doctor
text:
This is a crucial pivot point: your MRCP and tumor markers are normal, which effectively rules out a stone obstruction or a common malignancy like pancreatic or cholangiocarcinoma cancer. Since your ultrasound shows an enlarged, thin-walled gallbladder but no stones, and you have a history of heavy alcohol use, we must determine if this represents acute acalculous cholecystitis or severe alcoholic hepatitis with cholestasis. Have you developed a fever or chills in the last 24 hours, and does pressing on the right side of your abdomen cause sharp pain?

REQUEST TEST: C-Reactive_Protein
REQUEST TEST: Prothrombin_Time

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: C-Reactive_Protein: Normal; Prothrombin_Time: Normal

speaker: Doctor
text:
The normal CRP and Prothrombin Time, combined with normal MRCP and tumor markers, effectively rule out acute cholecystitis, biliary obstruction, and common malignancies. With your history of heavy alcohol consumption and a "thin-walled" gallbladder on ultrasound that persists without stones, this is highly suspicious for acute acalculous cholecystitis or severe alcoholic hepatitis with cholestasis. Do you have a known history of gallstones, and have you experienced any recent viral illnesses or rapid weight loss?

REQUEST TEST: Abdomen_CT_With_Contrast (focused on liver parenchyma and gallbladder wall)

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: CT_Abdomen_With_Contrast: No acute findings; Ultrasound_Gallbladder_Duplicate: Enlarged, thin-walled gallbladder. No evident stones.

speaker: Doctor
text:
I see the CT and ultrasound confirm a thin-walled, stone-free gallbladder despite your significant alcohol history and cholestasis. Given the normal inflammatory markers and lack of obstruction, does your jaundice improve with fasting or worsen after eating fatty foods?

REQUEST TEST: Serum_Protein_Electrophoresis
REQUEST TEST: Alpha_Fetoprotein

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Serum_Protein_Electrophoresis: Normal; Alpha_Fetoprotein: Normal

speaker: Doctor
text:
The normal protein electrophoresis and alpha-fetoprotein rules out primary liver cell carcinoma and multiple myeloma. With persistent cholestasis, a thin-walled gallbladder, and no obstruction, I suspect severe alcoholic hepatitis or infiltrative disease like sarcoidosis. Do you have a history of diabetes, and do you have a dry cough or shortness of breath?
